claims.text: An intact, self-forming passive film provides effective corrosion protection to the high-entropy alloy in a chloride-rich environment.
Chloride-rich solutions are aggressive toward passive films.
Controlled reciprocating sliding in a chloride electrolyte can be combined with in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy.
Passive-film integrity is the structural mediator governing the coupled tribo-corrosion response.
Mechanical sliding disrupts and damages the passive film.
Wear-induced passive-film damage causes localized passive-film breakdown.
Passive-film disruption exposes fresh underlying metal to the corrosive electrolyte.
Exposure of fresh metal elevates the corrosion rate during sliding relative to static corrosion.
The combined tribo-corrosion degradation exceeds the sum of isolated wear and static corrosion effects.
Tribo-corrosion produces a higher total degradation rate than the matched static-corrosion condition.
The corrosion component is significantly higher under sliding than under static conditions because of passive-film disruption.
Wear rate may increase because the damaged passive film no longer protects the substrate effectively.
The prediction should hold at sufficient chloride concentration and moderate-to-high wear stress when the passive film is mechanochemically vulnerable.
Increasing chloride concentration can further deteriorate passive films and worsen corrosion.
Rapid passive-film self-repair may prevent the predicted coupled degradation response.
Wear energy that is too low to disrupt the film may prevent the predicted response.
Microstructural strain hardening and localized passivation kinetics may compete with the proposed film-disruption mechanism.

The hypothesis would be falsified if sliding caused no statistically significant corrosion-current increase, no detectable passive-film compromise, or no excess degradation beyond additive wear and corrosion.

contradictions.description: The baseline and experimental design specify only combined sliding-plus-corrosion and static-corrosion groups, but the falsification rule requires comparison with the sum of isolated wear and static corrosion. An isolated-wear control is therefore invoked by the decision rule but absent from the stated controlled comparison.
